item.title: New study maps India’s diverging fire regimes
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Conservation, Fires, Forest Fires, and Forests
item.description: New research from the Centre for Wildlife Studies evaluated changing fire regimes in wildlife reserves across three Indian landscapes, finding that burned area rose most steeply in the Eastern Ghats between 2002 and 2022, at 9.3% per year. The rising fires in the Eastern Ghats show that it has a more fire-prone combination of vegetation, […]
item.content:encoded: New research from the Centre for Wildlife Studies evaluated changing fire regimes in wildlife reserves across three Indian landscapes, finding that burned area rose most steeply in the Eastern Ghats between 2002 and 2022, at 9.3% per year. The rising fires in the Eastern Ghats show that it has a more fire-prone combination of vegetation, climate, and repeated human ignition than the Western Ghats, while Central India sits in between. The study evaluated roughly 20,000 square kilometres of protected forest land across 13 reserves. Both human and climate factors explained between 21 and 77% of annual fire activity across individual reserves, with drought and community fire use both playing major, but regionally varying roles. A region- and reserve-specific deconstruction of forest fires is essential to understanding how different rainfall, temperature, and land use regimes, as well as population densities, affect fire occurrence, the researchers argue. For example, high human population density was strongly associated with more frequent fires in Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary (Telangana) and Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (Andhra Pradesh), but in Nagarahole and Bandipur National Parks (Karnataka), similar conditions were linked with fewer fires. “Various factors could be contributing to this paradoxical trend in burned areas in India, including forest management, land-use change, changes in fire ignitions, anthropogenic climate change and natural climate variability,” the study says. Using satellite-derived burned-area data from NASA’s MODIS sensor, the study found that burned area in the Western Ghats declined by 10.8% per year. item.title: The endurance runner of the grasslands
item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Grasslands, Mammals, and Wildlife
item.description: A creature of the open grasslands, the blackbuck’s evolutionary survival trick is endurance — it can sprint incredibly fast.
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. A creature of the open grasslands, where there’s nowhere to hide, the blackbuck’s evolutionary survival trick is endurance — it can sprint incredibly fast, sometimes even fast enough to have once outrun the Asiatic cheetah when it still prevailed in India. The blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra) is the sole living member of its genus. In a 2025 story published in Mongabay-India, Mihir Godbole, founder of The Grasslands Trust-India, said: “Blackbucks … are key indicators that grassland species cannot do well in any other habitats.” Female blackbucks are light brown and live in herds, sometimes led by a mature male. Younger males live in bachelor groups until they mature, at which point they establish their own territories, develop a black-brown coat, and grow corkscrewed horns. During mating season, males form display territories called leks, leaping and calling to attract females. Once spread across the Indian subcontinent, blackbuck populations were decimated by trophy hunting under British rule. The species is now extinct in the wild in Pakistan and Bangladesh and survives in small protected pockets in Nepal, while the majority live in India. A 2016 estimate put the Indian population at roughly 35,000. They live in the open grassland habitats and are found across 13 states, with strongholds in Velavadar, Tal Chhapar, Point Calimere, and Karnataka’s Ranebennur and Jayamangali reserves. The IUCN lists the blackbuck as least concern, indicating that its population is widespread and abundant. In India, it’s protected under Schedule I…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: India’s new climate targets must navigate geopolitical uncertainty [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Pallavi DasVaibhav Chaturvedi
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Clean Energy, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environment, Environmental Economics, Fossil Fuels, Global Warming, Green Energy, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Impacts of Climate Change, Oil, and Renewable Energy
item.description:
- India’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution targets 60% non-fossil power capacity by 2035.
- Studies suggest India’s non-fossil fuel capacity could reach 60-68% by 2035, depending on economic growth, demand-side savings, and the cost of solar panels.
- High oil and gas prices could speed up electrification and strengthen the case for clean power capacity.
- The views in the commentary are those of the authors.
item.content:encoded: Well past the summer peak, India’s power system remains under strain. The country met daytime demand of over 267 GW even in September, yet fell short by more than 7.7 GW after sunset, when solar generation tapers off. India may have withdrawn its bid to host COP33 in 2028, but COP31, which opens in Antalya on November 9, will be the first UN climate summit since India submitted its 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). It raises the bar for climate ambition, targeting 60% non-fossil installed capacity by 2035 and relying heavily on the power sector to drive the transition over the next decade. Climate impacts are rising in India and worldwide. The world will likely cross the 1.5°C threshold in the next few years, as per a recent UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report. The margin by which this threshold is breached before accelerated mitigation efforts bend the temperature curve again will determine how catastrophic climate impacts become. All countries must double down on mitigation now. Yet India’s 2035 NDC targets are being tested in real time, as rising demand, especially in non-solar hours, pushes for all available options, including fossil energy. At the same time, annual power demand could still be hit if India’s economic growth slows because of global conflict, trade disputes, supply chain concentrations, energy inflation, and the impact of artificial intelligence. The clean energy transition risks losing momentum just as it needs to accelerate. A target built for uncertainty India’s current position reflects both progress and credibility.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: New-to-science seahorse is one of three long-misidentified species
item.dc:creator: Ananya Singh
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Ecology, Fish, New species, Oceans, Wildlife, and Wildlife Trade
item.description:
- Scientists have identified a new seahorse species, Hippocampus amandavincentae, from the Indian Ocean, based on two specimens collected from trawler bycatch in Tamil Nadu.
- The discovery has helped resolve over a century of taxonomic misidentification by revealing that the thorny seahorse, earlier believed to be a single species – Hippocampus histrix, is actually three distinct species.
- As indiscriminate fishing and illegal trade threaten seahorse populations, the study’s findings contribute to a clearer picture of spiny seahorse diversity in the Indo-Pacific region.
item.content:encoded: Scientists have identified a new-to-science seahorse species from the Indian waters, which has helped resolve the taxonomy of a group misidentified for over a century. In 1856, zoologist Johann Jakob Kaup described the thorny or spiny seahorse, Hippocampus histrix, based on samples from Japan. Since then, this seahorse has been thought to be a single, widespread species ranging from the Red Sea, through the Indian Ocean to Japan, Indonesia and the Pacific Islands. Over 150 years later, in 2019, a team of researchers collected two seahorse specimens from trawler bycatch that landed at the Thoothukudi Fisheries Harbour in Tamil Nadu. After studying their morphology and genetic data, and comparing them with samples housed in museum collections around the world, the researchers realised that these two specimens represented a distinct lineage. Their study, published recently in Zootaxa, confirmed what was once thought to be H. histrix is not one, but three separate species—Hippocampus histrix in the Pacific Ocean, Hippocampus jayakari in the Arabian region, and the newly described species from the Indian Ocean named Hippocampus amandavincentae, whose population had long been clubbed with H. histrix. The findings provide a better understanding of spiny seahorse diversity in the Indo-Pacific region. “This discovery shows that identification and understanding species is the first step towards protecting them and their habitat,” said Shalu Kannan, the study’s lead author and a project scientist at the Zoological Survey of India, Andaman and Nicobar Regional Centre. item.title: One orangutan goes home. Will the five babies follow?
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Endangered species, Mammals, Pet Trade, Primates, Wildlife, Wildlife Trade, Wildlife Trafficking, and Zoos
item.description:
- An orangutan seized from a Mumbai apartment in 2024 is being repatriated to Indonesia after two years of delays over health and procedural issues.
- The juvenile will be sent to a rehabilitation centre in Sumatra, where experts say he could be prepared for release into the wild in a few years.
- Indonesia is also seeking the repatriation of five baby orangutans rescued in Odisha, whose origins and suspected trafficking are under investigation.
item.content:encoded: Two years since an infant orangutan was seized from a Mumbai apartment, the procedures are finally complete to repatriate him to his homeland, Indonesia. The animal will fly out of India on October 19, 2026, after a long bilateral process, delayed by procedural hurdles and poor health condition of the animal, according to Yogesh Nilkand Warkad, the assistant management authority of CITES, Mumbai, who is overseeing the operation in India. In the meantime, the infant orangutan, who was estimated to be around one year at the time of seizure from a private apartment in Dombivli, Mumbai, was transferred to Gorewada zoo in Maharashtra in consultation with the then Chief Wildlife Warden Vivek Khandekar, Warkad informs. Then, due to poor health from a respiratory issue when he was just one and a half years of age, he was transferred to Vantara zoo in Gujarat, for subsequent rehabilitation. He was recuperating there, as per the authorities. “This is the first successful repatriation of a seized CITES animal from India and my office (Asst. Management Authority CITES) did everything in our capacity to make it happen,” Warkad informs Mongabay-India over the phone. Mongabay-India has previously reported on the increasing smuggling of non-human primates, particularly apes, into India, primarily by air from Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia. Beyond violating CITES regulations, the trade threatens already critically endangered species such as orangutans with further population declines in their native habitats. It also raises serious ethical concerns, given the complex social bonds of these animals…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Small-scale fisheries a big threat to rays
item.dc:creator: Rupsy Khurana
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Environment, Environmental Politics, Fish, Fishing, Natural Resources, Oceans, Wildlife, Wildlife Protection Act, and Wildlife Trade
item.description:
- A study documenting manta and devil ray landings across a decade in a coastal area in Tamil Nadu reveals declining populations and fewer adult rays.
- The proportion of adult spinetail devil rays in marine species brought to shore fell from 64% to 26% over the study period. With rays producing just one pup every two to three years, the loss of breeding adults makes population recovery more difficult.
- Though all 10 species of manta and devil rays were listed under CITES Appendix I in November 2025, prohibiting commercial international trade, the restrictions do not cover domestic catches and trade.
item.content:encoded: Manta and devil rays, collectively known as mobulids, are large cartilaginous fish known for their broad, wing-like pectoral fins, which help them glide through the water. They often feed on zooplankton and small crustaceans and fish in shallow coastal waters, making them vulnerable to entanglement in fishing nets. Roughly 259,000 mobulids are killed each year in fisheries, globally. Five countries — India, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Peru — account for 87% of these deaths, which are mostly attributed to small-scale fisheries. India is the highest contributor, accounting for 28.2% deaths. Limited catch data and inadequate understanding of the impacts of small-scale fisheries make it difficult to assess the status of these species. Increasing fishing pressure puts several ray species at risk of population collapse. To address this gap, a group of researchers tracked mobulid bycatch from fishing boats in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, between 2013 and 2023. Their study, published in Conservation Science and Practice, found evidence of declining populations of four species — the spinetail devil ray (Mobula mobular), the sicklefin devil ray (Mobula tarapacana), the oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris), and the bentfin devil ray (Mobula thurstoni). The study notes that these population declines occurred alongside increasing fishing pressure, suggesting overfishing as the likely cause. “Counting the number of mobula rays caught is always confusing,” said Divya Karnad, a senior lecturer at the University of Exeter and an author of the study. Because the research team wanted to track real changes in the population, they divided the catch…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Two new-to-science subterranean fishes reveal a hidden world underneath
item.dc:creator: Monish Upadhyay
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.reporting-project: Almost Famous Species and Beyond Protected Areas
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Fish, Groundwater, New species, Positive Environmental, Research, Villages, Water, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Researchers have described two new subterranean species, Gitchak nakana (a transparent, blind loach) and Rakthamichthys anchi (a transparent, blind swamp eel), from wells in Assam.
- Deeper groundwater systems in Assam and northeast India are only partially mapped and remain poorly understood beyond 200 m depth, experts say.
- Any impacts observed on surface water percolate into the groundwater impacting subterranean species. Therefore, it is crucial to monitor habitats and keep a check on pollution, researchers warn.
item.content:encoded: A decade ago, Wimarithy K. Marak, a resident of Assam’s Goalpara district, often used to encounter a small pink creature in her neighbourhood’s wells. She simply thought of it as a worm infesting her locality. In 2021, after she became a researcher, she stumbled upon the creature again while drawing water from a well. “This time I sent the picture to my supervisor and we brought a specimen to the lab,” she says. The creature turned out to be a two-centimetre long blind loach with a body so transparent that its blood and internal organs give it a striking blood-red appearance. The first specimen was collected in March 2021. Although further explorations into neighbouring wells yielded no results for the now described Gitchak nakana, the team of researchers had requested village residents to alert Marak if they came across anything unusual in their wells. Much later in 2024, when one of Marak’s relatives was cleaning his well, he came across what seemed like a worm. “My relatives had fully drained the well and that is when they found a  specimen of another subterranean species,” she says. Named Rakthamichthys anchi, the holotype, measuring around 310 mm, was collected in May 2024. R. anchi is a slender eel-like fish which shares characteristics with Gitchak nakana. Researchers then published two papers earlier this year describing both the species. item.title: As the Ganga treaty nears expiry, renewed concerns over water sharing arise
item.dc:creator: Umesh Kumar Ray
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Drought, Environment, Environmental Politics, Rivers, and Water
item.description:
- As the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty with Bangladesh nears renewal, Bihar wants to resolve its demand for a fixed share of Ganga water during the lean period first.
- Experts do not buy Bihar’s claim that the treaty burdens the state. They say the real issue is siltation caused by the Farakka barrage.
- Experts suggest Bihar made a stakeholder and that its concerns over water availability, siltation and erosion can be addressed through a basin-wide approach.
item.content:encoded: As the Ganga water-sharing treaty between India and Bangladesh ends this year, Bihar seeks to resolve its long-standing demands before the treaty is renewed. The treaty, signed in December 1996, governs the sharing of the Ganga river’s water between upstream India and downstream Bangladesh, particularly during the lean season when river flows are low. Under the treaty, during the lean period from January to June, if water at the Farakka barrage is less than 70,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs), India and Bangladesh each get half. If the water at the barrage is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh will be assured 35,000 cusecs, and the rest will go to India. If the water is 75,000 cusecs or more, India will get an assured 40,000 cusecs, and Bangladesh will get the rest. The agreement further says Bangladesh will get a guaranteed flow of 35,000 cusecs on the first and last ten days of April and 27,633 cusecs between April 11 and 20. If the Ganga’s flow falls below 50,000 cusecs in any ten-day period, the two governments will enter immediate consultations to make emergency adjustments. For decades, Bihar’s political leaders have argued that the Ganga water-sharing treaty with Bangladesh does not adequately account for the state’s water needs. Sanjay Jha, a member of parliament from Bihar’s ruling party Janata Dal United, said on August 6 during the Zero Hour in Rajya Sabha that renewing the treaty without adequately incorporating Bihar’s long-term water security, development needs, and water resource requirements would…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Light may influence morning basking behaviour in captive gharials
item.dc:creator: Lekha Bandopadhyay
item.author: Arathimenon
item.reporting-project: Almost Famous Species and Beyond Protected Areas
item.topic-tags: Animal Behaviour, Animals, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Encroachment, Endangered species, Endemic species, Environment, Protected Areas, Reptiles, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A study on captive gharials suggests light could be a stronger cue than temperature for morning basking movements, particularly among young gharials.
- Researchers call for studies on wild gharials to understand how light affects basking behaviour.
- With a species recovery score of just 19%, habitat protection remains crucial for both wild gharials and captive-reared individuals reintroduced into rivers.
item.content:encoded: Like all crocodilians, Gangetic gharials regulate their body temperature using external heat sources. They warm their enormous bodies, which can grow to 15 to 20 feet in length, by basking on sandbanks, making it an important daily activity. Both temperature and light are important environmental cues for basking. However, a recent study on captive Gangetic gharials (Gavialis gangeticus) finds that light is a stronger cue than temperature for their morning basking movements. The researchers expected natural light to be a reliable indicator for gharials to determine the right time to bask on land, says Megha Khanduri, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki, Finland. However, artificial lighting at night and the resulting light pollution can disrupt the relationship between natural light and temperature in the environment. The study finds that if light is the more dominant cue for basking, this disruption could lead gharials to bask at the wrong time, when air temperatures are not warm enough, or choose suboptimal basking sites. “Such behaviours could be potentially life-threatening as it can result in hypothermia,” says Khanduri. “If hatchlings leave the water earlier than the adults because of differences in sensitivity to light, it could also expose them to terrestrial predators in the early hours.” Radiant cue for basking The study was conducted on 382 captive gharials raised from eggs and housed in enclosures at the Deori EcoCentre in Madhya Pradesh. item.title: Invaders get better at competition in introduced ranges: Study
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Divya Kilikar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Environment, Forests, Plantations, and Plants
item.description: Are invasive plants better at competing with species in places they invade than species in their native range? A paper investigated this using Erigeron canadensis, commonly known as Canadian horseweed, to find that plants from non-native populations had 19.2% higher competitive ability than those from native populations. In the study, that advantage was evident across […]
item.content:encoded: Are invasive plants better at competing with species in places they invade than species in their native range? A paper investigated this using Erigeron canadensis, commonly known as Canadian horseweed, to find that plants from non-native populations had 19.2% higher competitive ability than those from native populations. In the study, that advantage was evident across two watering conditions — watered and drought. Although drought reduced competitive ability overall by 12.9%, the difference between native and non-native populations was not significant. Canadian horseweed is native to North and Central America that has spread widely across Europe, Asia and other regions. In some introduced areas, it can suppress other plant species and reduce local plant diversity. The researchers conducted a large glasshouse experiment involving plants from 100 native and 165 non-native populations of Erigeron canadensis. They grew the plants under different conditions, including adequate water and drought, and tested how they performed when growing alone, alongside individuals of their own species, and alongside other plant species. The paper suggests that the competitive advantage evolved independently in different regions. Genetic analyses identified four clusters, but increased competitive ability was evident in two. The result suggests that similar evolutionary changes can emerge independently rather than being explained solely by the spread of one already competitive lineage. One of the crucial findings was that the advantage was associated with interactions with other species, rather than competition between individuals of the same species. item.title: Noise pollution is a public health risk that’s hard to measure and monitor
item.dc:creator: Disha Shetty
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Environment, Environmental Politics, Health impacts, Human Rights, and Pollution
item.description:
- Noise pollution is an environmental stressor linked to health impacts.
- Large-scale measurement of noise pollution is difficult due to the nature of sound and limited access to acoustic models, leaving gaps in data on noise in Indian cities.
- In some cities, citizen groups have been demanding action against noise pollution, building political pressure. Enforcement of rules is key to progress, say activists.
item.content:encoded: A recent debate over using DJs and high-powered sound systems during Pune’s Ganesh festival brought noise pollution and its health impacts into focus. In August and September, residents and citizen groups in Pune called for stricter enforcement of noise limit rules, prompting a parliamentary committee review of noise and light pollution. The National Human Rights Commission also sought a report from Maharashtra’s pollution control board on action taken on noise limit violations during the festival. The impact of urban noise extends beyond festivals. Prolonged exposure to environmental noise is linked to sleep disturbance, hearing impairment and cardiovascular risks, making noise pollution a public health concern in India’s increasingly noisy cities. Gaps in noise pollution data from Indian cities and the challenges of monitoring sound levels at scale are compounding the problem, say researchers. Meanwhile, citizens have been pushing for better policy and better implementation of guidelines, with incremental changes being observed over the years, say noise pollution activists. Under-researched “silent killer” “It’s been known for a long time that noise is more than just a nuisance or an annoyance, but that it’s a serious cardiovascular disease concern,” said Danielle Vienneau, Associate Professor at the UMC Utrecht in The Netherlands, an expert on environmental pollution and its impact on human health. item.description: On October 11, the Upper Siang district administration issued an order prohibiting the assembly of five or more people amid intensifying protests against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). The order was issued two days after four protesters were detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014. Protests against the 11,000 MW hydropower […]
item.content:encoded: On October 11, the Upper Siang district administration issued an order prohibiting the assembly of five or more people amid intensifying protests against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). The order was issued two days after four protesters were detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014. Protests against the 11,000 MW hydropower plant turned violent earlier this month after Chief Minister Pema Khandu’s visit to the district. Residents of the Siang, Upper Siang, and East Siang districts have consistently opposed the development of the dam, which will submerge 27 villages, including Upper Siang’s district headquarters, Yingkiong. On October 13, three civil society groups — the Adi Banne Kebang United, Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum Youth Wing, and SUMP Affected Area Youth Association (SAAYA) submitted a memorandum to the Upper Siang District Collector condemning police atrocities and demanding the immediate release of those arrested for protesting. Police allegedly lathi charged protesters on October 4, days after protesters set fire to vehicles and stormed an MLA’s house. The memorandum demands the unconditional release of protesters from police custody, the “immediate and complete withdrawal of Central Armed Police Forces from Siang and Upper Siang,” a halt on all studies being done to determine the dam’s viability in the area, and the quashing of all legal proceedings against protesters. “Failure to comply will compel the youth and public to escalate democratic agitation, for which the district administration and law enforcement authorities shall be held solely responsible,” says the memorandum, seen by Mongabay-India.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Divya Kilikar
item.topic-tags: Animals, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Endemic species, Environment, Mammals, Wildlife, Wildlife Protection Act, and Wildlife Sanctuary
item.description: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. During the monsoon this year, sloth bears seemed to quite literally unearth an unusual prey in the forest floor of Amrabad Tiger Reserve, Telangana: shield-tailed snakes. Researchers studying over a hundred scat samples found the remains of the snake in a handful – potentially the […]
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. During the monsoon this year, sloth bears seemed to quite literally unearth an unusual prey in the forest floor of Amrabad Tiger Reserve, Telangana: shield-tailed snakes. Researchers studying over a hundred scat samples found the remains of the snake in a handful – potentially the first record of the bears hunting the snake. The shaggy-coated and long-clawed sloth bear (Melursus ursinus) is a mostly nocturnal mammal that is native to the Indian subcontinent. It has a long, flexible snout and mobile lips that enable it to suck up ants and termites. While they love their occasional meat tidbits, they mostly thrive on insects, fruits and wild berries. Sloth bears usually live in rugged terrain with rocky hillocks and dense scrub vegetation. Like other bears, they depend on dens as safe spaces for resting and raising their cubs. They can adapt to life in a wide range of habitats such as dry grasslands, scrublands, and moist tropical forests. The only population estimation of sloth bears in India stems from a 2006 survey: between 6,000 to 11,000 sloth bears, with around half of them living outside protected areas. The IUCN Red List classifies the species as vulnerable, which means it faces a high risk of extinction in the wild. In India, it receives the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Sloth bears may be helping regenerate forests by dispersing viable seeds. item.title: Lessons from translocating a tiger for population recovery [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Samir Kumar Sinha
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Big Cats, Biodiversity, Cats, Himalayas, and Tigers
item.description:
- A three-year-old tigress has been translocated from Bihar’s Valmiki Tiger Reserve to Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal.
- Valmiki was once considered a punishment posting for forest staff and had only a handful of tigers. It can now spare animals for other reserves.
- Prey recovery, community support, and safe connectivity will determine whether the translocated tigers can establish a breeding population in their new home.
- The views in this commentary are that of the author.
item.content:encoded: The territory of the three-year-old tigress, known as T138, spreads across the grasslands east of the Pandai river in Bihar’s Valmiki Tiger Reserve (VTR). The area lies along the India-Nepal border and is part of the Chitwan-Parsa-Valmiki transboundary tiger landscape. The tigress stalked spotted deer and wild pigs yet rarely encountered people. Two decades ago, however, the landscape was far from ideal tiger habitat. The road from Manguraha, headquarters of the reserve’s easternmost range, to Gaunaha block headquarters passed through a three-kilometre stretch lined with stone crushers. Tractors carrying boulders extracted from the Pandai riverbed through legal and illegal mining operations filled the air with thick dust and the deafening noise of machinery. Tigers largely remained west of the river. Efforts to curb mining in the landscape formed part of a wider legal battle over forest conservation. A key intervention came through the Supreme Court’s proceedings in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India of 1995, a landmark case on forest conservation. In December 2002, the Court stayed a Ministry of Environment and Forests (MoEF) order restoring two mining leases within Valmiki Wildlife Sanctuary. In February 2005, it accepted recommendations by the Central Empowered Committee to stop mining inside national parks and wildlife sanctuaries and their safety zones. The Valmiki landscape, covered by Saccharum spontaneum grass, which provide good cover for tigers. Image by Samir Kumar Sinha. item.title: As Kashmir turns from paddy to apples, dependence on outside rice grows
item.dc:creator: Farzana Nisar
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Environmental Economics, Food, Himalayas, Mountains, and Plantations
item.description:
- Kashmir’s agricultural landscape is shifting from paddy towards higher-value horticulture, especially apple cultivation.
- The decline in paddy cultivation is increasing the region’s dependence on rice supplied from outside, raising questions about the region’s long-term food security.
- Experts say the challenge is to balance farmers’ economic gains from horticulture with the need to retain enough paddy land to protect against future food and climate risks.
item.content:encoded: “Twenty years ago, all this was paddy,” says Nazir Ahmad, a farmer from Qaimoh, a village in south Kashmir’s Kulgam district, pointing at the rows of apple saplings that now cover his land. Today, much of that landscape has changed. The irrigation channels set up for paddy still exist, running through the fields as they always have. However, the paddy they once fed has given way to apple plantations. Across Kashmir, farmers are increasingly replacing food crops with horticulture, especially apple orchards, as they seek higher returns amid rising cultivation costs. For many growers, the calculation is straightforward. Paddy offers modest returns, while apples, particularly high-density plantations, promise significantly higher earnings. The move makes economic sense for individual farmers. However, this is now leading to Kashmir Valley becoming increasingly dependent on outside states for its staple food — rice. Nisar Ahmed from Kulgam district in Kashmir, used to cultivate paddy on his nine-kanal (0.46 hectares) farmland, which earned him between ₹30,000 and ₹50,000 annually. A few years ago, he converted the land into a high-density apple orchard because he was facing losses. After the shift, Nisar and his family saw a considerable increase in their earnings. “Every season, we earn around ₹4 lakhs to ₹5 lakhs (₹400,000-500,000),” he said. Fareed Ahmed Wagay, a farmer who converted six kanals (0.30 hectares) of paddy land into an apple orchard also said that paddy cultivation could not fetch healthy returns. “As a result, hundreds of farmers are now shifting towards horticulture and planting…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Reclaiming nature’s many delights through living fences [Book Review]
item.dc:creator: Usha Rai
item.author: Renuka Kulkarni
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Cities and Towns, Plantations, Plants, and Trees
item.description:
- Planted hedges have been integral to the landscape in India and around the world, but have been changed and reduced due to urbanisation.
- The book The Living Fence is a guide to all those who yearn for the peace and beauty of green spaces, and who’d like to build small biodiversity refuges in their compound walls.
- Based on five years of travel and research by landscape architect Sonali Dahotre, the book is a collection of photographs, field observations, and ecological notes on over 250 plant species in India, highlighting their ecological roles and their potential in supporting biodiversity.
item.content:encoded: My neighbour in Gurugram has a hedge of roses and jasmines outside the brick wall of her house. Just before the rains it is fragrant with white jasmines and in the winter season there are clusters of small pink and white roses on the hedge. My house, also in Gurugram, has a hedgerow of hibiscus trees outside a brick and grill fencing. The trees are uneven and in the flowering season, which is almost round the year, there are red, orange and pink hibiscus flowers. Both the hedge and the hedgerow attract squirrels, butterflies and birds. I have seen bulbuls nesting in the thickest parts of the hedgerow. In the hot summer months, many people put earthen pots of water for birds and squirrels adjacent to the fencing or in courtyards. There were also chameleons, before Gurugram became highly urbanised. During the rainy season, I have also seen many snakes in the undergrowth. A few months ago, I spotted one in the tree fencing that separates my house and my sister’s. The adjoining tall and stately kanak champa (Pterospermum acerifolium) also in the fenced area, is home to many birds and bees, the latter occasionally building their honeycombs in them or the adjoining tall trees. These fences, teeming with life, still exist at a time when floods, climate change and the rampant growth of brick and concrete buildings and industrial hubs are decimating our rural and urban landscapes and eating into the spaces of birds, bees and a myriad other creatures…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Ganges river dolphins may synchronise their activity with time, tides and the moon
item.dc:creator: Sneha Mahale
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.reporting-project: Almost Famous Species and Beyond Protected Areas
item.topic-tags: Animal Behaviour, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Endemic species, Mammals, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A new month-long study used underwater acoustic recordings to study Ganges river dolphins in West Bengal’s Rupnarayan river.
- Dolphin detections peaked at dawn and dusk. Tidal height showed a stronger relationship than the time and lunar cycle.
- While the study covered only one lunar cycle and did not measure prey availability, the findings could help improve dolphin surveys by incorporating more drivers in monitoring.
item.content:encoded: In the tidal waters of West Bengal’s Rupnarayan river, Ganges river dolphins live with constantly shifting water levels, currents and conditions. A new study in the river found that tide, time of day and lunar cycle influences when the dolphins were detected. Published in Aquatic Mammals, the month-long study examined the these parameters together in relation to acoustic detections (monitoring the animal by the sounds it makes) of Ganges river dolphins. At the study site, tides rise and fall twice a day with occasional tidal bores, causing large shifts in water levels and the currents, explains Gargi Roy Chowdhury, principal project associate at Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and the first author of the study. “It is a human-modified landscape with intense motorised fishing, and industrialised lower reaches with the Kolaghat thermal power plant downstream of the study site. It holds a good population of dolphins,” she adds while noting that large vessel traffic is limited here. A river shaped by the tide The Rupnarayan is an 85-km-long tributary of the Hooghly, influenced by tides from the Bay of Bengal, about 220 km away. Its upper reaches have narrower channels, while the lower stretches are wider. The river also experiences periodic tidal bores, and its flow is shaped by both seasonal and tidal forces. item.title: As El Niño strengthens, coral reefs face narrow windows for recovery
item.dc:creator: Max Martin
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Coral Reefs, Ecology, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Fish, Global Warming, and Oceans
item.description:
- Repeated marine heatwaves are hitting reefs before they can fully recover, raising the risk of long-term decline.
- Since 1998, every strong El Niño has coincided with a global coral bleaching event, and each event has affected more reef areas than the last.
- Indian reefs show sharply different responses across regions, highlighting the role of local conditions and the need for sustained monitoring of the 2026–27 El Niño.
item.content:encoded: As UN Secretary-General António Guterres says, El Niño is being “supersized” by a warming climate. The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) warns that coral reefs are being hit by new bleaching events before they have had time to recover from earlier ones. UNEP likened reefs to “an overmatched boxer” taking repeated blows, citing findings from the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) of the International Coral Reef Initiative (ICRI). The outlook is stark. “Multiple lines of evidence indicate that the majority (70-90%) of warm water (tropical) coral reefs that exist today will disappear even if global warming is constrained to 1.5°C,” as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change warns. The headline, however, is that marine heatwaves are narrowing the window for coral reef recovery. “Coral reefs once had decades to recover after major bleaching events. Today, they’re lucky to get five or six years,” said Manuel González Rivero, a reef expert at The Australian Institute of Marine Science and lead author of the GCRMN report. “And for many reefs affected by the unprecedented marine heatwaves in 2024, this year’s El Niño likely means they’ll have had little more than a year to begin recovering before being hit again.” “India’s own reefs show the same trend,” said marine biologist Amruth P., assistant professor in the Department of Life Sciences at CHRIST University, Bengaluru. “A 24-year study in Lakshadweep recorded coral cover falling from about 37% to under 20% since 1998 after repeated marine heatwaves.” The study by the Mysuru-based Nature Conservation Foundation…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: The emotional cost of displacement
item.dc:creator: Arathi M.R.
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Coast, Coastal erosion, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Fishing, Floods, Health impacts, Human Rights, Oceans, People, and Villages
item.description:
- Coastal erosion is creating a prolonged state of displacement and insecurity among the fishing communities in Kerala’s Thiruvananthapuram.
- A study suggests Thiruvananthapuram’s coast has lost over 2.6 sq km of land to coastal erosion over a 14-year period.
- The government rehabilitation scheme separates community members from each other and their livelihoods leading to social, economic and psychological distress.
item.content:encoded: “This was our home,” says 43-year-old Baby Titus, pointing to a green-painted house secured with a rusty lock. Waves were repeatedly crashing on the right side of the house. “The sea kept entering and receding, and it caused a short circuit inside the house. You would get an electric shock wherever you touched.” A road past Kollamkode Church in Thiruvananthapuram leads to the Arabian Sea, where rows of houses like Titus’s line the shoreline. Many houses here have been engulfed by the sea. The remains of those houses, along with the granite boulders dumped into the sea for a seawall, are constantly battered by the waves, each surge crashing against them with a frightening roar. Kulathoor grama panchayat is the southernmost grama panchayat in Thiruvananthapuram district in Kerala. Its coastal wards, including Pozhipallivilakam, Mullassery, Kollamkode, Paruthiyoor, Pozhikara Beach and Pozhiyoor, have been facing severe coastal erosion for decades. Many of these wards have only seven or eight rows of houses remaining, out of about 100. Of those that remain, only a few are inhabited. Fearing the house was structurally precarious and hence, unsafe, Baby Titus now lives in a rented two-bedroom house next door with her husband and three adolescent children, paying ₹2,000 a month. The house’s owners have moved elsewhere due to flooding. Baby Titus spends the night listening anxiously to the sound of every crashing wave, wondering whether the sea is coming in — a reality shared by the families living along the coast. item.content:encoded: A new paper documents the first known record of a moth using the umbilicate lichen, Lasallia pertusa, as a camouflage background. Published in the journal Arthropod-Plant Interactions, the observation was made in July 2025 at Duggi, in Kugti Wildlife Sanctuary, Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh, at about 3,200 m elevation. Lichen-associated camouflage has been documented before, including in moths. In this case, however, the association involves an umbilicate (attached to its substrate only at a single point), foliose (with flat, leaf-like lobes) lichen, rather than the more commonly documented crustose or bark-growing lichens. The finding, therefore, expands the range of lichen growth forms known to potentially participate in insect camouflage. It also points to the fact that a seemingly inconspicuous lichen can be an important part of an animal’s visual environment and survival strategy. One of the authors, Sanjay Kumar Uniyal, informs Mongabay-India that though there have been similar observations of moths mimicking lichens in the past, this particular lichen species has been documented for the first time. “This might have an evolutionary consequence which can only be understood through further studies,” Unniyal shares. L. pertusa has a large, perforated and highly irregular thallus (vegetative body), providing a particularly complex visual background, reports the paper. The moth that belongs to the family Noctuidae, was found resting directly on the lichen growing on exposed rock. The moth’s identification was based on photographs and expert examination.
